headline: Samsung unveils Flex Titanium display for next-gen foldables: 20x stiffer, less crease
summary: Samsung's new Flex Titanium display tech, featuring a titanium alloy film and plate, promises 20 times greater mechanical stiffness and a less noticeable crease. It will debut in the next Galaxy foldables at Unpacked on July 22.
details: Samsung has officially introduced its new Flex Titanium display technology, set to debut with the next generation of Galaxy foldable devices. This innovation promises a more durable display with a significantly less noticeable crease. The new foldables are expected to be unveiled at Samsung's Unpacked event on July 22.

The technology incorporates a titanium alloy film positioned beneath the OLED panel, which boosts the display's mechanical stiffness by 20 times. This film works in conjunction with a titanium plate underneath, providing stable support when the device is unfolded.

The titanium plate also maintains the necessary flexibility for repeated folding, eliminating air gaps through advanced hole processing technology. Kyung-Jin Yoo, EVP for Samsung Display, highlighted that "micro-patterned holes" in the folding section ensure both flexibility and robust durability.

Early glimpses at CES this year showcased Samsung's "seamless" foldable display exhibit, which featured a device with an invisible crease. This demonstrated a significant improvement over older display tech. A leaked video, purported to be the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, also suggests a very smooth screen with no visible crease.
caption:

headline: Vint Cerf is working on a plan to unleash AI agents on the open internet
summary: Internet pioneer Vint Cerf is advising Innovation Labs on an open architecture to identify and hold AI agents accountable. This initiative aims to use DNS infrastructure to ensure trust and transparency as AI agents operate more autonomously online.
details: Vint Cerf, a co-architect of the internet, has joined Innovation Labs as an advisor, a subsidiary of Identity Digital. Their goal is to develop an open architecture that allows AI agents to identify themselves and be held accountable on the internet.

Innovation Labs proposes DNSid, a registry system designed for agent identification. This system links each AI agent to an existing internet domain name and uses cryptographic proofs to log its registration over time, addressing the current lack of a shared identification standard.

Cerf highlights the increasing importance of naming and identification for AI agents, particularly regarding their authorities, accountability, and trustworthiness. While most AI agents currently operate within proprietary systems, businesses anticipate a future where they interact autonomously across the internet.

The initiative aims to avoid the pitfalls of proprietary standards by not owning registration data or engaging in other AI business. Cerf suggests that widespread adoption of any protocol will ultimately depend on user pressure, similar to how TCP/IP gained traction.

Cerf acknowledges the challenges ahead, describing the period as both "fascinating" and "exasperating" due to the dramatic power of AI agents. He believes the agentic economy is a likely, though not inevitable, future driven by human preference for automation.
